1.word_for_word: sapta-triṃśe — in the thirty-seventh chapter; hate keśini — when Keśī had been killed; acyutaḥ — Acyuta; bhāvi-karmabhiḥ nāradena stutaḥ — praised by Nārada for deeds yet to come; krīḍan vyoma-asuram avadhīt — while playing, killed the demon Vyoma; vṛṣa-veṣa-asuram yadvad keśinam haya-veṣiṇam — just as the bull-disguised demon, so Keśī disguised as a horse; kaṃsa-prāṇa-sakham — Kaṃsa's intimate companion; hatvā kaṃsam vyasum iva akarot — by killing him, made Kaṃsa as though already lifeless; mahā-hayaḥ — a gigantic horse; mahīm nirjarayan — loosening and tearing the earth; saṭābhiḥ — with his mane; avadhūtāni abhrāṇi vimānāni ca — clouds and aerial cars tossed about; heṣitaiḥ — by neighing; akhilam viśvam bhīṣitam — the whole world terrified
1.translation: In the thirty-seventh chapter, after Keśī was slain, Nārada praised Acyuta for deeds that were still to come, and Kṛṣṇa later killed the demon Vyoma while engaged in play. Just as he had killed the demon who came in the form of a bull, he killed Keśī, who came in the form of a horse. Keśī was so close to Kaṃsa that by killing him Kṛṣṇa made Kaṃsa seem already bereft of life. In the first verse Keśī is introduced in this form, and the second states that the Lord called him to battle. As a gigantic horse he loosened and tore the earth beneath him. His mane hurled clouds and celestial vehicles here and there, filling the sky with confusion, and his horse-like neighing terrified the entire world.

2.word_for_word: tad-dheṣitaiḥ — by those neighings of his; atiniṣṭhuraiḥ — exceedingly harsh; bālaiḥ puccha-lomabhiḥ — by the hairs of his tail; vighūrṇitāḥ ambudāḥ — clouds were whirled around; ājau — for battle; agraṇīḥ — advancing to the front; upāhvayat — called him near; keśī tat niśamya — Keśī hearing that; mṛgendra-vat nādam akarot — roared like a lion
2.translation: His neighing was exceedingly harsh, and the hairs of his tail whirled the clouds about. ‘In the contest’ means for battle. Kṛṣṇa came forward and called Keśī toward himself. Hearing this, Keśī gave a roar like a lion.

3.word_for_word: mukhena kham piban iva — as though drinking the sky with his mouth; mukham vivṛtya — opening his mouth wide; abhimukhaḥ abhijagāma — came directly toward him; aty-amarṣaṇaḥ — exceedingly enraged or unable to tolerate him; pratyak yad-bhyām jaghāna — struck at him with his two hind legs; durāsadaḥ — impossible for others to overcome; duratyayaḥ — difficult to resist when charging; caṇḍa-javaḥ — of fierce speed
3.translation: Seeing Kṛṣṇa, Keśī came straight at him with his mouth gaping as though to swallow the sky. ‘Aty-amarṣaṇa’ means that he was furiously enraged and unable to tolerate Kṛṣṇa. He struck at him with his two hind legs. He was ‘unassailable,’ impossible for others to overpower, and when he charged he was exceedingly difficult to withstand because his speed was fierce.

4.word_for_word: tad-hananam vañcayitvā — evading that attack; hananāya prasāritayoḥ pādayoḥ — the legs extended to strike; hastābhyām gṛhītvā — seizing them with his hands; parividhya bhrāmayitvā — whirling him around; vyavasthitaḥ — remained standing in place
4.translation: Kṛṣṇa evaded the blow, seized with both hands the legs Keśī had stretched out to strike him, whirled him around, and then remained standing where he was.

5.word_for_word: vyādāya mukham — opening his mouth wide; vegena harim prati ādravat — rushed swiftly toward Hari; hariḥ hasan — Hari, smiling; uttaram savyam bhujam — his left arm; yathā uragam bile — like a serpent entering a hole
5.translation: Keśī opened his mouth and rushed violently toward Hari. Hari merely smiled and put his left arm into the demon's mouth, just as a serpent enters a hole.

6.word_for_word: dantāḥ — the teeth; carvaṇāya bhagavad-bhujam spṛśanti — touching the Lord's arm in order to bite it; vyādānena vivṛtāḥ — exposed by the opened mouth; ayaḥ — iron; tapta-mayam — intensely heated metal; spṛśantaḥ yathā — as when touching it; āmayaḥ — dropsy, abdominal swelling
6.translation: The verse next describes his teeth: exposed by his gaping mouth, they touched the Lord's arm in an attempt to bite it, but it was as though they had touched red-hot iron. The comparison with ‘āmaya’ refers to dropsy or abdominal swelling.

7.word_for_word: leṇḍam — dung; purīṣam — feces; utsṛjan — discharging

8.word_for_word: karkaṭikā-phalam — a cucumber-like fruit; pakvam sādyantam vidīrṇam — when ripe, split from end to end; tadvat vidīrṇāt dehāt — from his body split in that manner; vyasoḥ — bereft of life; avismitaḥ — not astonished, free from pride; ayatnena hataḥ ariḥ yena — he by whom the enemy was killed without effort; kaṃsāya kṛṣṇam ādiśya — having informed Kaṃsa about Kṛṣṇa; tad-rahasya-ādi-paiśunaiḥ — by disclosing that secret and related matters; kaṃsa-ghāta-ādi kṛṣṇasya kāryam āvedayan — announcing Kṛṣṇa's future work beginning with Kaṃsa's death
8.translation: A ripe karkaṭikā fruit splits from end to end; Keśī's body likewise split apart, and he was left lifeless. Kṛṣṇa remained ‘unastonished,’ that is, free of pride, for he had killed the enemy effortlessly. Nārada, having disclosed to Kaṃsa the secret concerning Kṛṣṇa, now announced to Kṛṣṇa the work he would perform, beginning with the killing of Kaṃsa.

9.word_for_word: devarṣiḥ ity-ādinā — beginning with ‘the divine sage’; na ayam sūcakaḥ — he is not a malicious informer; kintu sarva-suhṛt — rather, a friend of all; bhāgavata-pravaraḥ — foremost among devotees
9.translation: This is introduced with ‘the divine sage.’ One should not think that Nārada was a malicious informer; rather, the description ‘foremost among the Bhāgavatas’ shows that he is the friend of everyone.

10.word_for_word: asmat-rahasyam vairiṇi kaṃse sūcitavān iti mā śaṅkīḥ — do not suspect that he revealed our secret to the enemy Kaṃsa improperly; tvam īśvaraḥ — you are the Lord; bhū-bhāra-daitya-saṃhārāya avatīrṇaḥ — descended to destroy the demonic burden of the earth; tad-anurūpa-ācaraṇena viśvam paripālaya — protect the universe by acting accordingly; aprameya-ātman — O immeasurable Self; aparicchinna-rūpa — of unlimited form; yogeśa — Lord of yoga; acintya-prabhava — of inconceivable power; jagad-īśvara — ruler of the universe; vāsudeva — present in all beings; akhila-āvāsa — shelter of all; sātvata-pravara — foremost of the Sātvatas; prabho — O all-powerful Lord
10.translation: Do not suppose that Nārada's disclosure of the secret to the enemy Kaṃsa was improper. The sense of his prayer is: ‘You are the Lord who has descended to destroy the demons who burden the earth; therefore protect the world by acting in accordance with that purpose.’ There can be no real fear for you: ‘O immeasurable Self’ means one whose form is unlimited; ‘Lord of yoga’ means one whose power is inconceivable; ‘Lord of the universe,’ its controller; ‘Vāsudeva,’ present within all beings; ‘abode of all,’ the shelter of everything; ‘foremost of the Sātvatas’; and ‘Prabhu,’ the all-powerful Lord.

11.word_for_word: tvam ātmā — you are the Self; na jīva-vat paricchinnaḥ — not limited like an individual jīva; sarva-bhūtānām āntaraḥ ekaḥ anusūtaḥ ātmā — the one Self pervading the interior of all beings; edhasām antar jyotiḥ iva — like fire within pieces of wood; gūḍhaḥ — hidden; guhā-śayaḥ — dwelling within the cave of the intellect; sākṣī — witness; mahā-puruṣaḥ — the Great Person; īśvaraḥ — the Lord; īśvaram vinā paratantrāṇām jīvānām pravṛttiḥ na ghaṭate — dependent jīvas could not act without the Lord
11.translation: If one asks how he is of this nature, Nārada says, ‘You are the Self.’ Kṛṣṇa is not limited like an individual living being; he is the single inner Self threaded through all creatures, like fire latent within pieces of wood. Yet although he dwells in beings, they do not see him, for he is hidden. He lies deeper even than the intellect, as the indwelling Lord of the cave; he is the witness, and a witness is not itself the object seen. He is the Great Person and therefore cannot be comprehended by limited minds. What proves that he is within all? The term ‘Lord’: the activity of dependent living beings cannot be accounted for without the governing Lord.

12.word_for_word: aham īśvaraḥ anyat sarvam īśitavyam — I am the Lord and everything else is governed; ātma-āśrayaḥ — resting on oneself; sva-tantraḥ — independent; sādhanāntara-nirapekṣaḥ — requiring no other instrument; māyayā śaktyā — through the power called māyā; guṇān sasṛje — created the guṇas; taiḥ guṇaiḥ idam viśvam sṛjasi atsi saṃharasi avasi — by them you create, consume/dissolve and protect this universe; satya-saṅkalpaḥ — whose resolve is unfailing; saṅkalpa-eka-sādhye — accomplished merely by resolve; bahiḥ-sādhana-apekṣā na — no external instrument is required
12.translation: How is it established that he is the Lord while all else is governed by him? He is self-dependent and independent, requiring no instrument besides himself. Through his power, māyā, he creates the guṇas, and through those created guṇas he creates the universe, consumes or dissolves it, and protects it. One might object that acts such as creation normally require a full complex of agents and instruments. The answer is ‘whose resolve is true’: when something is accomplished by his resolve alone, no external instrument is required. Thus he is the Lord.

13.word_for_word: prastutam āha — he states the present matter; sa tvam iti — with ‘that very you’; bhū-dhara-bhūtānām — of those who bear the earth; bhuvam dharanti iti bhū-dharāḥ — kings are ‘earth-bearers’ because they support the earth; rājānaḥ tad-rūpāṇām — kings in those forms
13.translation: Nārada now turns to the matter at hand with the words ‘that very you.’ ‘Bearers of the earth’ means kings, since kings are those who sustain the earth; the reference is to those who have assumed such royal forms.

15.word_for_word: paraśvaḥ ahani — on the day after tomorrow; adya eva akrūraḥ eṣyati — Akrūra will arrive today itself; śvaḥ mathurām gantāsi — tomorrow you will go to Mathurā; paraśvaḥ cāṇūra-ādīn tvayā nihatān drakṣyāmi — the day after tomorrow I shall see Cāṇūra and the others killed by you; siddhavat nirdeśaḥ — statement as though already accomplished; vijñapana-prakāra-viśeṣaḥ — a special mode of respectful announcement
15.translation: ‘The day after tomorrow’ is to be understood as follows: Akrūra will arrive today, tomorrow you will go to Mathurā, and the following day I shall see Cāṇūra and the others killed by you. Nārada speaks of the future as though it were already accomplished; this is a particular manner of presenting his respectful announcement.

16.word_for_word: tasya anu — after that; tad-anantaram — subsequently; śaṅkha-ādīnām — Śaṅkha and the others; śaṅkhaḥ pañcajanaḥ — Śaṅkha is Pañcajana; vadham drakṣyāmi — ‘I shall see their killing’ is supplied; bhāvi-nirdeśa-mātram — merely an indication of future events; na tu ānantaryam vivakṣitam — immediate chronological succession is not intended
16.translation: ‘After that’ means subsequently. ‘Śaṅkha’ refers to Pañcajana, and the omitted sense is ‘I shall see the killing of Śaṅkha and the others.’ This is only a prediction of future events; the text does not intend that every event listed will occur immediately after the preceding one.

18.word_for_word: bhāryayā jāmbavatyā saha — together with his wife Jāmbavatī; sva-dhāmataḥ — from his own abode; mahā-kāla-purāt — from the city of Mahākāla
18.translation: The reference is to Kṛṣṇa together with his wife Jāmbavatī, returning from his own divine abode, the city of Mahākāla.

20.word_for_word: dvārakām āvasan — dwelling in Dvārakā; dvārakāyām vasan — residing in Dvārakā; kartā — ‘the doer’; kariṣyati — ‘he will do’
20.translation: ‘Dwelling in Dvārakā’ simply means residing there. The future sense of ‘kartā’ is ‘he will do.’

21.word_for_word: amuṣya — of this; viśvasya — universe; bhū-bhārasya vā — or of the burden of the earth
21.translation: ‘Of this’ may refer to the universe, or specifically to the burden of the earth.

22.word_for_word: amuṣya — of this; viśvasya — universe; bhū-bhārasya vā — or of the burden of the earth
22.translation: Again, ‘of this’ may mean ‘of this universe’ or ‘of this burden upon the earth.’

23-24.word_for_word: viśuddha-vijñāna-ghanam — a compact mass of perfectly pure consciousness; kevalam jñāna-eka-mūrtim — whose sole nature is consciousness; sva-saṃsthayā — by abiding in his own nature; paramānanda-rūpayā — whose nature is supreme bliss; samyak āptāḥ sarve arthāḥ yena — by whom all purposes are completely fulfilled; āpta-kāmatā — complete fulfillment of desire; amogha-vāñchitam — whose desire is never fruitless; sva-tejasā — by his own power; cit-śaktyā — by conscious potency; nitya-nivṛttaḥ māyā-kārya-rūpaḥ guṇa-pravāhaḥ yasmāt — from whom the stream of guṇas, the effect of māyā, is eternally excluded; īśvaram — the controller of others; sva-āśrayam — resting on himself; anyasya avaśam — not under another's control; ātma-māyayā — by māyā dependent upon himself; vinirmitā aśeṣa-viśeṣāḥ — all distinctions fashioned; dhuryam — foremost
23-24.translation: Having made this announcement and received the Lord's approval, Nārada bows to him in these two verses. ‘A compact mass of perfectly pure consciousness’ means one whose sole nature is consciousness. Because he simply abides perfectly in his own nature, which is supreme bliss, every purpose is already completely fulfilled in him. His complete fulfillment of desire is expressed by ‘whose wish is never fruitless.’ If desire exists, one might ask whether saṃsāra must therefore be unavoidable. No: by his own radiance—his conscious potency—the stream of guṇas, which is the product of māyā, is eternally absent from him. Therefore ‘we approach Bhagavān as shelter,’ the possessor of unsurpassed sovereignty. One might then ask: if Nārada knows past, present and future, how can he fail to know the Lord's cosmic manifestation, or call him untouched by the guṇas? The next verse answers: Kṛṣṇa is the Lord, the controller of others, dependent only upon himself and subject to no other. By his own māyā, which is itself under his control, all distinctions—beginning with the mahat principle, or including his varied manifestations among the Yadus and elsewhere—are fashioned. Nārada therefore bows to him as the foremost.

26.word_for_word: nāradena vyoma-vadhaḥ na dṛṣṭaḥ — Nārada had not seen Vyoma's killing; katham vyoma-vadha-prasaktiḥ — how then does the killing of Vyoma enter the narrative?; prātaḥ eva keśi-vadha-anantaram nāradena uktam aṅgī-kṛtya — after accepting Nārada's words in the morning immediately after Keśī's death; punaḥ tathā eva paśūn pālayatā vyomaḥ hataḥ — while again tending the animals as before, Kṛṣṇa killed Vyoma; yad vā — alternatively; vyoma-vadhaḥ pūrvam eva vṛttaḥ api — Vyoma's death had already occurred earlier; veṣa-dhāri-vadha-prasaṅgāt atra ucyate — it is narrated here because of the thematic connection with killing disguised demons; kecit śaṅkhacūḍa-vadhāt pūrvam eva paṭhanti — some recensions place it before Śaṅkhacūḍa's death
26.translation: One may ask: Nārada did not witness the killing of Vyoma, so why is Vyoma's death narrated at this point? The answer is that early in the morning, after Keśī had been killed and Kṛṣṇa had accepted Nārada's words, he again went on tending the animals as before, and Vyoma was then killed. Alternatively, Vyoma's death may already have occurred earlier but is narrated here because the subject is the killing of demons who assumed disguises. Some recensions in fact read this episode before the killing of Śaṅkhacūḍa. The narrative begins with ‘one day.’

28.word_for_word: meṣāyitān — those acting like sheep; meṣa-vat ācaritān — behaving as sheep; svayam cora-vat ācaritaḥ — himself acting as a thief; apovāha — carried away; apakṛṣya nināya — dragged off and took away
28.translation: ‘Those who had become sheep’ means those who were acting the role of sheep. Vyoma himself took the role of a thief and carried them away, dragging them off one after another.

29.word_for_word: pidadhe — he closed over; chāditavān — he covered or concealed
29.translation: ‘Pidadhe’ means that he covered over and concealed the opening.

30.word_for_word: śaraṇa-daḥ — giver of shelter; āśraya-pradaḥ — one who provides refuge; hariḥ siṃhaḥ iva — Hari like a lion
30.translation: ‘Śaraṇa-da’ means ‘the giver of shelter, the one who provides refuge.’ Hari is compared to a lion.

32.word_for_word: paśu-māram — as an animal is slaughtered; paśu-māraḥ yathā bhavati tathā — in the manner of killing an animal; aniḥśvāsam — without breath
32.translation: ‘Paśu-māram’ means ‘as an animal is killed’; the sense is that Vyoma was left unable to breathe.

33.word_for_word: paśu-māram — as an animal is slaughtered; paśu-māraḥ yathā bhavati tathā — in the manner of killing an animal; aniḥśvāsam — without breath
33.translation: The expression again means that he was killed like an animal and deprived of breath.

34.word_for_word: bhuvi — on the earth; gopaiḥ stūyamānaḥ — praised by the cowherds; upari — above; vaimānikaiḥ devaiḥ — by the gods in celestial vehicles
34.translation: On earth Kṛṣṇa was praised by the cowherds, while above he was praised by the gods riding in celestial vehicles.
